item.text: {"text":"Directional transition modeling has direct precedent in [TiCoSeRec, WSDM 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.01056v2): a weighted directed item-transition graph supplies collaborative information to a sequential attention model. [Denoising Dual Sparse Graph Attention, 2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10791-025-09532-2) likewise preserves click direction, uses separate incoming/outgoing adjacency matrices, and shares information across sessions. These support distinguishing ordered transitions from undirected affinity. A practical hypothesis—not an established result from these papers—is a lightweight SASRec residual scored with separate source and target embeddings, so s(i)ᵀt(j) can differ from s(j)ᵀt(i), trained only on chronological training-history pairs.\n\nFor sparse histories and popularity controls, [TCA4Rec, 2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-025-01184-9) combines popularity-aware asymmetric augmentation with two-stage contrastive learning; “asymmetric” here describes augmentation, not separate transition embeddings. [PR-entmax, October 2026 preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17823) incorporates a popularity prior into a sparse training objective, then removes the prior at inference. Useful experimental directions: regularize separate transition embeddings toward shared item representations, smooth rare-edge counts, and tune popularity correction against the common macro validation HR@10. Compare against symmetric and reversed-transition ablations to establish whether direction contributes. Observed transitions remain behavioral associations; they do not verify product compatibility, complementarity, causal effects, or user conformity."}
